analysis.one_liner: Exempts employees earning $40,000 or more a year from federal overtime and minimum wage protections.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in February 1997, referred to a House subcommittee, and never brought to a vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Labor Standards Act requires employers to pay at least the minimum wage and to pay overtime — one and a half times the normal rate — for hours worked beyond 40 a week. This bill would exempt from those requirements any employee earning $40,000 a year or more, counting bonuses and commissions toward that total. It would also loosen the rules for deciding who counts as an 'administrative' employee exempt from overtime, and it would apply retroactively to lawsuits still in court. The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers of white-collar workers. They could require employees earning $40,000 or more to work unlimited hours without paying overtime, and would face fewer lawsuits over how overtime exemptions are classified. The retroactive provision would let employers off the hook in pending wage cases.

how_it_helps.text: It exempts any employee whose annual compensation is at least $40,000 from the Fair Labor Standards Act's wage requirements, so employers would not owe overtime to well-paid salaried staff no matter how many hours they work. [S3]
Bonuses and commissions count toward the $40,000 threshold, which makes it easier for employers to push workers over the line and out of overtime eligibility. [S3]

It weakens the test for the 'administrative' overtime exemption by barring consideration of whether an employee's duties relate to the employer's business operations, reducing employers' exposure to misclassification lawsuits. [S2] [S3]
It applies immediately and reaches any wage lawsuit that has not reached final judgment, so employers could win pending overtime cases retroactively. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Workers earning $40,000 a year or more, including many middle-income employees. They would lose the right to overtime pay for hours beyond 40 a week, and those working long hours would see their effective hourly pay drop. Workers with overtime lawsuits pending would lose their claims.

drawbacks.text: Workers would lose overtime pay: an employee earning $40,000 who routinely works 60-hour weeks would no longer receive time-and-a-half for the extra hours, effectively cutting their pay for the same work. [S2] [S3]
The retroactive effective date would reach into pending lawsuits, changing the rules mid-case for workers already seeking back overtime pay. [S3]

Defenders would argue the current exemption tests, written in 1938, are outdated for today's salaried professionals and generate costly litigation, and that workers earning $40,000 are well paid and can negotiate their own hours. That view has force for genuinely senior professionals, but the flat salary threshold would also sweep in many ordinary supervisors, technicians, and office workers with little bargaining power.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow to employers in the form of lower labor costs and less litigation; the costs fall on the workers themselves. A blanket salary cut-off is a blunt instrument: it would strip overtime rights from many mid-level employees who have no real say over their hours, and the retroactive provision reaches into pending court cases. The bill was never debated in committee, so these tradeoffs were never weighed publicly.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in a House subcommittee from February 1997 until the Congress ended in January 1999 — no hearing, no vote, never moved.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Petri introduced the White Collar Reform Act on February 6, 1997, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. [S1] [S5]
Two weeks later it was sent to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it remained for the rest of the Congress; the full committee never acted and the House never voted on it. [S5]
It drew three cosponsors, all Republicans. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Salaried workers earning around $40,000 or more kept their overtime protections, because the bill died in committee. Employers did not get the exemption they sought.

for.name: Rep. Thomas E. Petri
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 6, 1997 and gave introductory remarks on the floor. [S1] [S4] [S5]

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee / Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or reported the bill; after referring it to the subcommittee on February 21, 1997, no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Republicans; the bill was a single-sponsor measure that never attracted broader support on either side. [S4]

industries.industry: Employers of salaried white-collar workers (offices, banks, insurers, and other businesses with salaried staff)
industries.note: The bill would let them work employees earning $40,000 or more unlimited hours with no overtime pay, and would cut their exposure to misclassification lawsuits, including ones already in court. The savings come directly out of workers' pay for long hours.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' employment lawyers and workers with pending wage-and-hour claims
industries.note: The retroactive effective date would apply the new exemption to lawsuits not yet decided, eliminating many pending overtime claims. [S3]
